summary: This is the community around justcallmekoko, the creator of the popular ESP32 Marauder WiFi/Bluetooth pentesting firmware, whose channel also covers guns, general tech, and 3D printing. People show off builds, ask for help flashing and using Marauder-based hardware, and chat about maker/hacking projects more broadly. It suits hobbyists into ESP32 hardware hacking and 3D-printed gadgets, though it is not a narrowly focused infosec-only server.
red_flags: Content mixes in guns/firearms topics unrelated to security, which may surprise a purely infosec-seeking newcomer

summary: Red Team Alliance is a professional training and certification company (Covert Entry Associate/Professional/Expert) focused on physical red teaming, lock bypass, and covert entry, and this Discord is the community for their students and instructors. Conversation centers on physical security, breaking into buildings legally as part of engagements, and their courses/tools, so it fits people already working in or pursuing red team/physical pentest careers more than absolute beginners. They also sell training and hardware tools through affiliated storefronts.
red_flags: Commercial training company runs the server, so expect some promotion of paid courses/tools

summary: This is the official support server for Bruce, an open-source ESP32 firmware (maintained by BruceDevices/GitHub contributors like bmorcelli) that packs offensive-security tools such as WiFi deauth/evil portal, BLE attacks, Sub-GHz RF, and NFC/RFID into portable hardware like M5Stack and LILYGO devices. People come here to get help flashing and using the firmware, troubleshoot hardware, and share builds; it's aimed at people already comfortable with ESP32 hardware hacking rather than complete newcomers. It also promotes an official storefront selling a companion device (RF REAPER).
red_flags: Some offensive-security tooling (deauth, evil portal) can be misused; devs state it's for authorized testing only

summary: High Code is the community around a Brazilian-made multi-tool hardware device positioned as an alternative to the Flipper Zero, used for RF/RFID/NFC and general hardware-hacking experimentation. Members discuss the device's firmware, hardware mods, and use cases, largely in Portuguese given its Brazilian origin. It suits people already interested in Flipper-style pentesting gadgets rather than absolute beginners to security.

Hak5 is a long-running (since 2005) pentest-hardware company known for the WiFi Pineapple, USB Rubber Ducky, Bash Bunny, and other physical-access hacking tools, and this Discord-verified server is where pen-testers, students, and hobbyists talk tech, get help with Hak5 gear, and follow their podcast/video content. It's welcoming to a wide range of skill levels since Hak5's own material spans introductory to advanced. A solid general hub for anyone into pentest hardware, not just Hak5 product owners.

Nyan Devices builds beginner-friendly, menu-driven wireless security research gadgets, notably the nyanBOX, aimed at making WiFi/RF hacking approachable without deep coding knowledge. This Discord is where users get setup help, discuss firmware features, and share what they've built with the devices. It's a good fit for newcomers to hardware/wireless hacking looking for an easier on-ramp than fully DIY ESP32 projects.

This is an unofficial fan/support hub for Pwnagotchi, the open-source Raspberry Pi gadget by evilsocket that uses AI to capture WiFi handshakes for WPA cracking. People share builds, firmware tweaks, plugins and troubleshoot hardware here, alongside chatting about the wider WiFi-hacking hobby. Good fit for hobbyists building or customizing their own Pwnagotchi unit, though it's unofficial (the project's own community lives on its forum and Slack).
run_by: community-run (fan server, not evilsocket's official channel)
red_flags: Unofficial — the official Pwnagotchi community uses a forum (community.pwnagotchi.ai) and Slack, not this Discord

summary: Run around Iceman, maintainer of the widely-used Iceman fork of the Proxmark3 firmware/client, this server is where RFID and NFC hackers get help with Proxmark3, Flipper Zero and Chameleon devices, share scripts, and discuss card/tag cloning and access-control research. It's a solid hub for anyone building RFID hacking skills, from curious beginners to people contributing firmware code, though the pace assumes you already know roughly what RFID/NFC hacking involves.

Phish Club is a volunteer-run 501(c)(3) nonprofit that runs hands-on cybersecurity workshops, CTF nights, mentorship, and social events aimed at making the field approachable and fun rather than intimidating. It's explicitly welcoming to all skill levels, from complete beginners and job-seekers to working professionals looking to mentor, with free membership and both online and in-person activity.

This small server (going by the name 'Hacker's Night Light' and its 'Offensive Appliances' branding) appears centered on building and modifying everyday hardware/gadgets into penetration-testing or red-team tools, in the DIY badgelife/hardware-hacking hobbyist vein. There's no public description or website found, so details are limited; it looks like a niche maker community for people already comfortable with electronics and offensive-security hardware projects rather than a beginner starting point.
red_flags: No public description or findable website/socials — limited information to verify legitimacy or activity level

summary: Netgotchi appears to be a small DIY hardware project/community (in the Pwnagotchi-style 'gotchi' gadget lineage) focused on a network-monitoring or network-scanning tablet-style device, where members discuss builds, firmware and troubleshooting. No official description or site was found, so this reading is based on the name and the small, low-traffic size of the server; it looks aimed at people already into DIY network/security gadgets rather than newcomers.
red_flags: No public description or findable official source — small, low-confidence read based on the name alone

summary: Airplanes.Live runs a free, community-fed ADS-B flight-tracking network built from volunteer SDR feeders, and this Discord is where feeder operators get help setting up receivers, discuss MLAT and coverage, and talk about the aircraft database and mobile apps. It's an adjacent SDR/aviation-tracking hobby rather than security-focused, and it's friendly to beginners setting up their first receiver.

This is the Discord home for the Apres-Cyber Slopes Summit, a small ski-town themed cybersecurity conference. Members use it to discuss the event, coordinate around the in-person gathering, and chat about general security topics between events. It suits people already interested in attending or who have attended a past Slopes Summit rather than newcomers looking for a general learning community.
red_flags: Very small server (119 members) with limited public information found; could not confirm an official website.

summary: BalCCon (Balkan Computer Congress) is a non-commercial, community-organized hacker conference held annually in Novi Sad, Serbia, run entirely by volunteers from the regional hacker community. The Discord is used to discuss talks and workshops (chosen through an open call for papers), coordinate the event, and keep the Balkan hacker/maker community connected year-round. It suits anyone interested in the Balkan hacking scene, from curious beginners to experienced researchers presenting talks.

BSidesSLC is a community-run, grassroots cybersecurity conference held in the Salt Lake City area (Sandy, Utah), with the tagline "For the People, By the People," and this Discord is also linked to sister events BSidesCache and BSidesRedRocks. People use it to talk about the annual conference's talks, hands-on workshops, and CTF contests, and to network with local security professionals year-round. It's a good fit for both newcomers curious about the field and working professionals in the Utah infosec scene.

This server is the shared home for two annual Charlotte, NC-area events, BSides Charlotte and FrostCon, both focused on cybersecurity education and community building. Members discuss talks, workshops, and logistics for the events and use the space to network with the local infosec community between conferences. It suits both newcomers wanting to break into security in the Charlotte region and established professionals.

BSides Columbus is an annual cybersecurity conference in Columbus, Ohio presented with support from GuidePoint Security and community sponsors, featuring talks, workshops, and hacking villages. The Discord is where attendees and local security folks discuss the event and stay connected with the Columbus infosec community year-round. It works for both beginners curious about the field and working professionals in the area.
run_by: BSides Columbus organizers (with GuidePoint Security support)

summary: BSides CT is an all-volunteer, community-run cybersecurity conference held annually at Fairfield University in Connecticut and running since 2011. The event features talks, workshops, hands-on demos, and a CTF competition, and explicitly welcomes speakers of all experience levels; the Discord is used to plan the event and keep the Connecticut infosec community connected between conferences. It suits students and newcomers as well as established local security professionals.

This is the year-round Discord for DEF CON Group 937 and BSides Dayton, a volunteer-run Dayton, Ohio infosec community that hosts local meetups plus the annual BSidesDayton conference (talks, villages, and a story-driven CTF). It suits anyone in the Dayton area who wants ongoing security chat and in-person events, not just conference-week visitors.

Run by the volunteer, 501(c)(3) nonprofit behind BSides DFW, a free annual security "unconference" in the Dallas-Fort Worth area (typically the first Saturday in November). The Discord is the year-round hub for the local community around the event, with talk announcements, CTF chatter, and general security discussion for professionals and newcomers alike.

Summit City Infosec is the community group behind BSides Fort Wayne, Indiana, running local security meetups and an annual BSides conference for the region. The Discord serves as a year-round gathering spot for area security folks to chat, plan meetups, and coordinate around the conference, welcoming both beginners and working professionals.
run_by: Summit City Infosec / BSides Fort Wayne volunteers

summary: This is the Discord for BSides Houston, the Houston-area chapter of the volunteer-run global BSides security conference series. It's a smaller, moderately active space for local infosec folks to chat and connect around the annual event, useful mainly for people in or visiting the Houston area.
red_flags: official site could not be confirmed reachable at time of research

summary: BSides Leeds is a UK security conference held in Leeds (next edition June 2027 at Cloth Hall Court), explicitly welcoming newcomers through industry veterans with talks, an AMA desk, and a badge challenge. The Discord is the community's ongoing chat space for attendees and locals, sponsored in part by companies like PortSwigger.

BSides Memphis is a 501(c)3 nonprofit, community-powered cybersecurity conference held annually in Memphis (next on October 3, 2026 at Epicenter Memphis). This is its small but active Discord for local networking and event chatter, suited to security professionals and enthusiasts in the Memphis area.

This is the Discord for BSidesMKE, the community-run BSides security conference in Milwaukee, Wisconsin. Members use it to coordinate around the yearly event (CFP, volunteering, sponsorships) and chat about local infosec between conferences. It suits anyone in the Milwaukee-area security community, from students to working professionals.
red_flags: small, low-activity server; official site currently just shows a placeholder page for the next event

summary: This is the Discord community tied to BSides Prague, a community-run BSides security conference in the Czech Republic. It's used mainly to coordinate and chat around the annual event and connect with the local Czech/Central European infosec scene. It suits security people in or visiting the region, at any experience level.

This is the official Discord for BSidesROC, the volunteer-run BSides security conference held annually near Rochester, NY (RIT Inn & Conference Center). People use it to follow CFP/volunteer/sponsor announcements, plan meetups, and talk security year-round with the local upstate-NY community. Good fit for students and professionals in the Rochester/Western NY area.

This is the Discord for BSides St. Pete, a community-driven cybersecurity conference on Florida's Gulf Coast run by the nonprofit Cyber Ohana Project. It draws 600+ attendees for talks and hands-on trainings each year, and members use the server to coordinate around the event, network, and talk shop with the Tampa Bay-area security community. Suitable for beginners through advanced practitioners.

This is the Discord for BSides Tampa, one of the larger and longer-running BSides conferences in Florida. It's the most active of the Florida BSides servers here, used for CFP/volunteer coordination, networking, and general security chat throughout the year, not just around the event. It suits anyone in the Tampa Bay security community, from students to seasoned professionals.

This is the Discord for BSides SWFL, a newer cybersecurity conference held at Florida SouthWestern State College that brings together industry professionals and students in Southwest Florida. It's a small, young community used for event coordination and local networking rather than heavy daily chat. Good fit for students and early-career people in the SWFL region.
red_flags: very new/small server, only one conference held so far (2025)

summary: This is the community server for CactusCon, a long-running (14+ years) volunteer-run hacker/security conference held each February in the Phoenix, Arizona area (Mesa). Members discuss the conference CFP, talks, and villages, and use the server to stay connected between events; it welcomes newcomers alongside working security professionals.

This is the community server for CanSecWest (secwest.net), a long-running, research-heavy security conference held annually in Vancouver, Canada, run by dragostech.com inc. (which also runs PACSEC and the Pwn2Own contest lineage). It skews toward vulnerability researchers, reverse engineers, and offensive security professionals rather than beginners.

This is the community server for CarolinaCon, a long-running, community/volunteer-run hacker and security conference held in North Carolina. Members use it to discuss talks, CFP, and villages and to stay in touch with the regional hacker scene between events.

This is the community server for CornCon, an annual cybersecurity conference in the Quad Cities area run by the nonprofit Docent, notable for pairing an industry/CISO track with youth-focused programs like a High School Cyber Career Day and Kids' Hacker Camp. It's a friendly, community-oriented space suited to students, career-changers, and working security professionals alike.

This is the community server for CypherCon, Wisconsin's largest cybersecurity and hacker conference, held each spring in Milwaukee. It covers a broad mix of security, hardware hacking, cryptography, and AI topics and explicitly aims to serve everyone from curious beginners to seasoned professionals.

This is the official, verified Discord server for DEF CON, the world's largest hacker conference, founded by Jeff Moss (The Dark Tangent) and run with an army of volunteer "Goons." It's a massive, year-round hub covering every DEF CON village and group, CTFs, and general hacker culture, with channels and communities ranging from total beginners to elite researchers.
run_by: DEF CON Communications, Inc. (Jeff Moss / "The Dark Tangent")

summary: Pacific Hackers Association is a Bay Area nonprofit hacker community that runs monthly meetups, the HackTheBay hackathon/CTF, and its own small conferences (PHACK, SunSecCon), plus a presence at RSA Conference. It suits people in or near San Francisco who want in-person meetups, mentorship, and hands-on CTF practice rather than just online chat.

Hardwear.io is a well-known hardware security conference and training series (with editions in the Netherlands, USA, and India) focused on chip-level security, embedded systems, IoT, and side-channel/fault-injection research. The Discord is where attendees, speakers, and hardware security researchers discuss talks, CTFs, and training; it leans technical and suits people already working in embedded/hardware security more than newcomers.

Hexacon is a single-track offensive-security conference in Paris built around vulnerability research and malware/exploitation topics, run by a committee of well-known infosec researchers with no corporate-sponsored talks. Its Discord is mainly for attendees and speakers of this ticket-limited (500 seats) event to coordinate and discuss deeply technical exploit-development and reverse-engineering content, not a place for beginners.
run_by: Hexacon organizing committee (incl. Jean-Baptiste Bedrune, Jiska Classen, Ophir Harpaz)

summary: JawnCon is a Philadelphia-area community security conference held at Arcadia University, covering cybersecurity, hardware hacking, AI governance, and general tech culture with CTFs, a lockpicking village, ham radio classes/exams, and a retro-tech show-and-tell. The Discord is where attendees and volunteers plan and chat between and during the yearly event, suiting locals interested in a smaller, community-run con.

LayerOne bills itself as Los Angeles' premier annual security conference, with talks on malware, cryptography, and ransomware alongside hands-on villages for hardware hacking, lockpicking, soldering, robotics battles, and a career village. The Discord serves attendees and volunteers coordinating around the yearly event, and welcomes students and hobbyists alongside working security researchers.

CyberV is a French cybersecurity association connecting students, professionals, and enthusiasts around projects and events, and it organizes the well-known leHACK conference (formerly Nuit du Hack) in Paris. The Discord hosts year-round French-language discussion, project collaboration, and event planning, suiting people in the French infosec scene from students to professionals.

exclude_reason: General maker/hobbyist Discord (Maker Faire Asheville) with no security or hacking focus.
summary: Community Discord for Maker Faire Asheville, a family-friendly local showcase of DIY electronics, crafts, and invention run by the Asheville Makers group. People share builds and coordinate around the annual faire. It suits general makers and families, not security-focused hobbyists.

exclude_reason: General maker/hobbyist community (Maker Faire Orange County) with no security or hacking focus.
summary: Discord for Maker Faire Orange County, a family-friendly maker showcase bringing together tech enthusiasts, artists, crafters, and DIY hobbyists of all ages. Members share projects and coordinate around the annual faire. It suits general makers and families rather than security-specific hobbyists.

Official Discord for NorthSec, a major Montreal-based security conference and one of the largest CTF competitions in the world, covering pentesting, network and application security, reverse engineering, malware, and cryptography. The community discusses talks, training, and the CTF (roughly 90+ teams compete each year), and stays active year-round between events. It suits people already comfortable with offensive security concepts more than absolute beginners.

exclude_reason: General maker/creator convention (robotics, DIY, YouTube creator culture) with no security or hacking focus.
summary: Discord for Open Sauce, a large annual maker/creator festival in San Mateo, California run by OS Productions, featuring hundreds of DIY projects and talks from YouTube creators like Mark Rober and Vsauce. Members chat about builds, the festival, and creator culture generally. It's a broad maker/creator community rather than a security one.

Discord for ComfyCon AU, a casual, community-run Australian infosec conference that partners with the beginner-focused PancakesCon on joint online programming. It's an explicitly low-pressure, welcoming space with talks, villages, and CTF-style activities aimed at people newer to the industry rather than seasoned specialists. Good fit for beginners in Australia/APAC time zones wanting an approachable entry point into the security community.
run_by: ComfyCon AU volunteers (in partnership with PancakesCon)

summary: Discord for QueenCityCon, a community-organized, multi-day cybersecurity conference in Cincinnati, Ohio built by industry volunteers and sponsors rather than a single company. The event runs breakout sessions, hands-on workshops, and a dedicated career village with resume help and mock interviews, and it's explicitly open to anyone curious about the field. It suits newcomers looking for a friendly regional on-ramp as well as working practitioners networking locally.

This is the year-round Discord home for RVAsec, an annual Richmond, Virginia infosec conference with talks, a CTF, and lockpicking. Between conference dates the server keeps the community connected with chat and meetup coordination, so it suits people already in or near the Richmond security scene rather than pure newcomers looking for tutorials.

SAINTCON is a volunteer-run, nonprofit cybersecurity conference held every October in Provo, Utah, and this Discord is its active year-round community hub. Members discuss security topics, coordinate local meetups, and follow sub-communities like AppSec, hardware hacking, and lock picking that mirror the conference's tracks and contests.

SecretCon is Minnesota's annual hacker and cybersecurity conference held in the Twin Cities each spring, covering hands-on hacking, AI security, privacy, and hardware across three speaker tracks and CTFs. This Discord is its community server, drawing security pros alongside curious builders and first-time hackers in that regional scene.
red_flags: Little independent verification found beyond the official site; server description on Discord was blank.

summary: ShellCon is an annual information security conference held in the beach cities near Los Angeles, streaming its main talks free on YouTube/Twitch while running paid hands-on workshops. This Discord is its year-round community server for attendees and speakers to keep talking shop between events.
red_flags: Official site's most recent detailed event info found was from 2021; unclear if conference is still running annually as of 2026.

summary: Crowd Supply is a crowdfunding and store platform for open-source hardware, and this Discord is where backers and makers discuss campaigns, ask questions about specific gadgets, and see new hardware projects (including plenty of security- and privacy-oriented devices like SDRs and pentesting tools) as they launch. It's a general hardware-maker community rather than a security-focused one, but security hardware enthusiasts will find kindred projects here.

The Vintage Computer Federation is a nonprofit dedicated to preserving computing history through museum exhibits, restoration workshops, and Vintage Computer Festival events across North America. This Discord is where retrocomputing enthusiasts chat, share restoration projects, and coordinate around those festivals; it's a hobbyist/preservation community, not a security-focused one, though many hardware hackers overlap here.

This is the community Discord for Wild West Hackin' Fest, run by the BHIS family of companies (Black Hills Information Security, Antisyphon Training, Active Countermeasures). People discuss talks, workshops, and trainings from the conference (held in Deadwood, South Dakota) year-round, network with other attendees, and get updates on new events like the upcoming Mile High 2027 conference in Denver. It suits anyone into offensive/defensive security who enjoys BHIS's approachable, hands-on teaching style, from newcomers to veterans.
run_by: BHIS family of companies (Black Hills Information Security / Antisyphon Training / Active Countermeasures)

summary: Official Discord for Blue Team Con, a Chicago-based conference focused on defenders (SOC analysts, detection engineers, incident responders). Members discuss conference talks, ask defensive-security questions, and connect with other blue-teamers between events. It's a good fit for people who want to focus specifically on defense rather than general or offensive security.
run_by: Blue Team Con organizers (community-run nonprofit conference)

summary: This is the official Discord for BSides Atlanta, a community-run annual security conference in Atlanta (2026 event at the Georgia Tech Hotel and Conference Center). Locals use it to discuss talks, coordinate volunteering, and network with the Atlanta infosec scene, including partner groups like Atlanta Women in Cyber. It suits anyone in or near Atlanta looking to connect with the regional security community, beginners included.

This is the Discord tied to the Open Source Hardware Association (OSHWA) and its annual Open Hardware Summit. It's not a security-focused server per se, but a hub for open-source hardware makers, certification-program participants, and summit attendees to share projects and discuss hardware design between events. It suits hardware hackers and makers more than dedicated security researchers, though there's overlap with hardware-hacking interests.
red_flags: Primarily a general open-hardware/maker community rather than security-specific; relevance to a cybersecurity directory is limited to hardware-hacking overlap.

summary: This is a long-running community Discord tied to REcon, a well-known reverse-engineering conference held in Montreal (with a sister event, REcon Brussels). People here discuss reverse engineering, binary exploitation, and malware analysis topics, and swap notes about the conference itself, which runs talks in both English and French. It's aimed at experienced reverse engineers and researchers rather than newcomers to security.
rules_note: Not officially linked from recon.cx itself; appears to be a long-standing but unofficial/community-run server rather than one operated directly by the conference organizers.

summary: This is described as the official Discord for RSTCON, a small hacking conference held in Savannah, Georgia. Members use it to discuss the conference and connect with the regional US security community; the server is fairly small, so activity is more modest than larger con servers. It suits people near coastal Georgia looking for a local infosec meetup community.
rules_note: Distinct from an unrelated Romanian 'RST Con' (rstcon.com), which has its own separate Discord.
red_flags: Official site content could not be verified (returned blank/empty on fetch); details rely on secondary listings.

summary: This is the Discord for THOTCON, a long-running nonprofit hacking conference held annually in Chicago (the venue is kept secret until the week of the event). The server is where attendees find event announcements, chat with other hackers, and keep in touch between conferences, and it suits anyone into the Chicago/Midwest hacker scene rather than pure beginners looking for structured lessons.

Run by Gerald Auger (the Simply Cyber YouTube channel and courses), this large community is built around helping people break into or grow a cybersecurity career, including career-changers and veterans with no IT background. Members swap study advice, resume/job help, and home-lab tips, get a weekly threat brief, and can join voice study sessions, making it one of the more explicitly beginner-oriented career-focused servers around.

BSides312 is Chicago's community-run BSides conference (organized by the Hak4Kidz nonprofit), held the day after THOTCON so attendees can make a full con weekend of it. The Discord is where locals discuss the event, its CTF, lockpicking village, and Linux village, and stay connected with the Chicago infosec scene year-round.

Despite the id, this invite actually belongs to Elbsides, a volunteer-run security conference in Hamburg, Germany, held annually with keynotes, talks, and workshops kept affordable through sponsorship rather than high ticket prices. The Discord is a small, mostly event-focused chat for attendees and the local European security community rather than a beginner-teaching space.
rules_note: Note: the source listing labeled this 'BSides Vilnius' but the linked Discord and site both point to Elbsides (Hamburg), not a Vilnius event.
red_flags: Naming mismatch between listing label and actual conference identified from the invite/site

summary: This server belongs to Hackers Guild PGH, a year-round Pittsburgh hacker community that also organizes the annual GuildCon conference. It's a hub for local meetups and event planning rather than a pure beginner-lessons server, though the guild itself is community-oriented and open to newcomers interested in the local hacking scene.
red_flags: Official site returned an error when fetched directly, so details were pieced together from listing notes

summary: This is the Discord for BSides Detroit (referred to in some listings as BSides Michigan), a community-organized security conference with an active volunteer staff team and a recurring annual schedule. The server serves as the year-round hub for the Detroit-area infosec community to discuss the event and stay in touch between conferences.

This is the community Discord for BSides Nashville, a volunteer-run, non-profit information security conference held in Nashville. People use it to get event announcements, schedule and ticket info, volunteer coordination, and general chat with other Nashville-area security folks. It suits locals interested in attending or volunteering at the conference more than year-round deep technical discussion.
red_flags: Only 126 members with modest activity; discord presence not confirmed on the official site itself.

summary: This is the official Discord for BSides Orlando, a community-run information security conference in Orlando, Florida, linked directly from the conference's own website. Members get conference announcements (next event September 26, 2026), can talk with other Florida-area security people, and coordinate around the annual event, with activity that appears to continue between conferences given the sizeable ongoing membership.

Try Hard Security (also known as HackNow) is a large community built around helping people break into cybersecurity careers for free, mixing students with working professionals who answer questions and offer mentorship. Typical activity is career advice, study support, and general chat rather than hands-on hacking challenges, making it a good fit for people just starting out or trying to land their first infosec job.

This is the official Discord for Black Hills Information Security (BHIS), a well-known security consulting and training company that publishes free webcasts, tools, and blog content. The server functions as a broad infosec hangout where members ask and answer questions across red team, blue team, and general security topics, with BHIS staff and a large community of practitioners participating. Its size and topic range make it useful for beginners through experienced professionals.

Dropout Phreaks is a large general-interest community for ethical hackers, coders, and tech hobbyists that runs live workshops and CTF events alongside everyday chat. It suits people who want an active, casual hangout to learn hacking basics and take part in occasional challenges rather than a highly structured curriculum.
red_flags: Limited independent information available beyond the Discord listing sites and a LinkedIn roundup; harder to verify who specifically runs it.

summary: This is the official Discord for John Hammond, a popular cybersecurity YouTuber known for CTF walkthroughs, malware analysis videos, and beginner-friendly security education. The community plays CTFs together, discusses his videos, and welcomes newcomers who are just starting to learn hacking and security concepts, fitting its stated goal of free cybersecurity education 'without the fluff.'

Red Team Village is a nonprofit that runs the offensive-security village at DEF CON (and appears at other cons like BSides), and its Discord is where that community lives year-round with workshops, CTFs, and short skill-building "tactics" on topics like red teaming, malware development, and reverse engineering. People come here for hands-on offensive security training and to connect with village organizers and volunteers. It suits those with some security fundamentals already looking to go deeper into red team tradecraft, more than absolute beginners.
run_by: Red Team Village (501(c)(3) nonprofit, DEF CON village)

summary: This is a community-run job board and support server focused entirely on helping people break into or move up in the cybersecurity industry. Members post and find openings, ask about resumes, certifications, and interview prep, and discuss career paths. It's aimed squarely at job seekers and career-changers rather than technical skill-building itself.
red_flags: Large member count relative to activity; job-board servers like this can attract low-effort recruiter spam so verify postings independently

summary: This is the official Discord for OffSec, the company behind Kali Linux and certifications like OSCP, OSWE, and OSEP. People use it to get help with OffSec courses and labs, discuss certification study strategies, and talk shop with other students and alumni pursuing hands-on penetration testing skills. It suits anyone working through OffSec's training pipeline, from PEN-100 beginners to advanced cert-holders.

CyberDrain is an open-source project and community started by Kelvin Tegelaar that builds tools for managing and securing Microsoft 365 tenants at scale (CIPP and related automation), aimed at managed service providers. The Discord is where MSP admins get support on those tools, troubleshoot multi-tenant Microsoft 365 security/compliance setups, and talk to the developers directly. It's really a support server for practicing MSP engineers rather than a general security-learning space, so it assumes solid Microsoft 365/IT admin background.

MSPs Я Us (linked via an "MSP Exchange" invite) is a community for people who run or work at managed service providers, covering the broader IT-and-security concerns of running client environments: RMM tools, backups, vendor comparisons, and security compliance for clients. It's adjacent to security rather than a dedicated infosec server, useful mainly to practicing MSP technicians and owners rather than newcomers to security. Limited public information was available beyond the Discord listing itself.
red_flags: Could not independently verify server contents beyond the listing description; low visibility into moderation and activity quality

summary: Security Weekly is a long-running cybersecurity podcast/media network (now part of SC World/CyberRisk Alliance, originally founded by Paul Asadoorian) producing shows on security news, pentesting, and enterprise security leadership. The Discord is the fan and listener community around those shows, where people discuss episodes, security news, and chat with hosts and each other. It suits people of any level who enjoy security podcasts and want to talk shop informally.

This is the official community for ANY.RUN, an interactive online malware sandbox used by SOC teams and analysts to detonate and study malware and phishing samples. People discuss sandbox findings, share malware analysis writeups, ask product questions, and follow threat intel news from the ANY.RUN team. It suits working analysts and researchers already familiar with malware analysis more than absolute beginners.

Root-Me is a free, community-run hacking and CTF-style learning platform (French-founded, bilingual French/English) with hundreds of practice challenges across web, crypto, reverse engineering, forensics and more. The Discord is where players discuss challenges, ask for hints, and talk about the platform's events and rankings. It suits people who want structured wargame-style practice, from newcomers working through easy challenges up to advanced players chasing rare validations.

This is Packt Publishing's Discord for readers of its security and networking books, where members discuss book content, ask technical questions, and talk shop with other IT/security professionals. It's more of a book-club-style companion community than a hands-on hacking space, tied to Packt's catalog rather than a single tool or CTF. It suits people already reading Packt security titles who want a place to ask questions and compare notes.
red_flags: Fairly small and low activity for its size (158 online of 3700 members); relatively niche/book-focused
